rough-skinned-newt._en_desc: The Rough-Skinned Newt is a highly toxic amphibian found along the Pacific coast of North America. They produce tetrodotoxin, the same toxin found in pufferfish, and advertise their toxicity with bright orange undersides.

alpine-salamander._en_desc: The Alpine Salamander is found in the mountains of central and southern Europe. Unlike most amphibians, they give birth to live young that have completed their development inside the mother's body.

great-crested-newt._en_desc: The Great Crested Newt is the largest newt species in Europe. Males develop a distinctive crest during breeding season and have a white flash on their tail. They are legally protected in many countries.

marbled-salamander._en_desc: The Marbled Salamander is a small, stocky salamander with distinctive white or gray crossbands on a dark background. Found in eastern North America, they are one of the few salamanders that guard their eggs.

long-toed-salamander._en_desc: The Long-Toed Salamander is a small salamander found across western North America. They have a characteristic stripe running down their back and long toes that give them their name.

slimy-salamander._en_desc: The Slimy Salamander is a medium-sized lungless salamander found in the eastern United States. They secrete a sticky white substance from their skin that helps deter predators.

red-salamander._en_desc: The Red Salamander is a brightly colored amphibian found in the Appalachian region of the eastern United States. Adults have a distinctive red to orange coloration with scattered black spots.

lesser-siren._en_desc: The Lesser Siren is a fully aquatic salamander with external gills found in the southeastern United States. They lack hind legs and can survive drought by burrowing into mud and entering a dormant state.

greater-siren._en_desc: The Greater Siren is a large, fully aquatic salamander with external gills found in the coastal plains of the southeastern United States. They lack hind limbs and can grow up to three feet long.

three-toed-amphiuma._en_desc: The Three-Toed Amphiuma is a fully aquatic salamander found in the southeastern United States. It has an eel-like body with three tiny, non-functional toes on each vestigial limb.

waterdog._en_desc: The Waterdog is a fully aquatic salamander found in eastern North America. Like the mudpuppy, it retains its external gills throughout life and is an important indicator of stream health.

spring-salamander._en_desc: The Spring Salamander is a large, robust salamander found in cold mountain streams of eastern North America. They have a distinctive salmon or orange coloration with dark reticulations.

cave-salamander._en_desc: The Cave Salamander is a brightly colored salamander with orange to red body and black spots. Found in caves and rocky areas of the eastern United States, they are excellent climbers.

arboreal-salamander._en_desc: The Arboreal Salamander is a lungless salamander found in the coastal mountains of California. They are excellent climbers, spending much of their time in oak trees and rock crevices.

ensatina._en_desc: The Ensatina is a colorful salamander found along the Pacific coast of North America. They are famous in evolutionary biology as an example of a ring species, with different color morphs forming a circle around California's Central Valley.

slender-salamander._en_desc: The Slender Salamander is a small, lungless salamander found in California. They have long, thin bodies and can coil into a spiral when disturbed or to prevent water loss.

ringed-salamander._en_desc: The Ringed Salamander is a large, dark salamander with yellow or white rings or spots. Found in the Ozark Plateau region of the United States, they are one of the few salamanders that breed in the fall.

flatwoods-salamander._en_desc: The Flatwoods Salamander is a small, threatened salamander found in the longleaf pine forests of the southeastern United States. They breed in temporary fishless ponds and are declining due to habitat loss.

dusky-salamander._en_desc: The Dusky Salamander is a medium-sized lungless salamander found in eastern North America. They are variable in color and pattern and are often found near streams and springs.

four-toed-salamander._en_desc: The Four-Toed Salamander is a small salamander found in bogs and wetlands of eastern North America. They are the only salamander in their range with four toes on their hind feet.

gulf-coast-salamander._en_desc: The Gulf Coast Salamander is a small salamander found in the coastal lowlands of the southeastern United States. They are often found in bottomland hardwood forests and can tolerate mildly saline conditions.

tropical-caecilian._en_desc: Tropical Caecilians are limbless, serpentine amphibians found in tropical regions of the world. They live underground or in leaf litter, feeding on small invertebrates, and are the least known order of amphibians.

boulengers-caecilian._en_desc: Boulenger's Caecilian is one of the largest caecilian species, found in South America. These burrowing amphibians have ring-like grooves along their body and tiny, non-functional eyes buried beneath the skin.

ringed-caecilian._en_desc: The Ringed Caecilian is a limbless amphibian found in South America and the Caribbean. They have a distinctive ring-like pattern on their body and use a chemosensory tentacle to find prey in the soil.

monarch-butterfly._en_desc: The monarch butterfly is one of the most recognizable butterflies in North America, known for its striking orange and black wing pattern. It is famous for its incredible long-distance migration across thousands of miles.

luna-moth._en_desc: The luna moth is a large, pale green moth with long tail-like hindwings. It is nocturnal and attracted to light, and adults do not feed, dedicating their brief adult lives entirely to reproduction.

atlas-moth._en_desc: The atlas moth is the largest moth species, with a wingspan that can exceed 12 inches. Its wings have snake-head-shaped tips that deter predators, and like other giant moths, adults do not feed.

swallowtail-butterfly._en_desc: The eastern tiger swallowtail is a large, bright yellow butterfly with distinctive black tiger stripes. It is one of the most common and recognizable butterflies in eastern North America.

hawk-moth._en_desc: Hawk moths, also known as sphinx moths, are powerful fliers with streamlined bodies. Many species have extremely long proboscises for feeding on deep-throated flowers while hovering.

painted-lady-butterfly._en_desc: The painted lady is one of the most widespread butterflies on Earth, found on every continent except Antarctica. It is a strong migrant and a common visitor to gardens.

blue-morpho-butterfly._en_desc: The blue morpho is a brilliantly iridescent blue butterfly found in tropical rainforests. Its metallic blue wings are visible from great distances and are produced by light diffraction rather than pigment.

glasswing-butterfly._en_desc: The glasswing butterfly has remarkably transparent wings with only a thin dark border. The transparency is caused by tiny nanopillar structures on the wings that prevent light reflection.

cecropia-moth._en_desc: The cecropia moth is North America's largest moth with wingspans reaching 7 inches. It has striking red, orange, and white markings and, like other giant moths, adults do not feed.

io-moth._en_desc: The io moth is a beautiful silk moth with large eyespots on each wing. Males are yellow while females are reddish-brown, and both sexes flash their eyespots when threatened.

polyphemus-moth._en_desc: The polyphemus moth is a large, tan-colored silk moth with distinctive eyespots on its hindwings. It is named after the Cyclops of Greek mythology due to the large eyespots.

viceroy-butterfly._en_desc: The viceroy butterfly closely resembles the monarch and was long thought to be a mimic. It is now known to be somewhat distasteful to predators, making it a Müllerian mimic.

red-admiral-butterfly._en_desc: The red admiral is a striking black butterfly with bold red-orange bands and white spots. It is a strong flier found worldwide and often visits rotting fruit and tree sap.

great-spangled-fritillary._en_desc: The great spangled fritillary is a large, orange butterfly with distinctive silver-spotted underwings. Its larvae feed on various violet species while adults nectar on milkweed and coneflowers.

clouded-yellow-butterfly._en_desc: The clouded yellow is a bright golden butterfly common across Europe and parts of Asia. It is a strong migratory species that sometimes appears in large numbers in areas outside its normal range.

comma-butterfly._en_desc: The comma butterfly has uniquely ragged wing edges that help camouflage it as a dead leaf. It has a distinctive white comma-shaped mark on its dark brown underwings.

mourning-cloak-butterfly._en_desc: The mourning cloak is one of the longest-lived butterflies, surviving up to 11 months. It overwinters as an adult and is often the first butterfly seen in spring, with dark wings bordered in yellow.

zebra-longwing-butterfly._en_desc: The zebra longwing is a distinctive butterfly with black wings marked by pale yellow stripes. It is unique among butterflies in that adults can digest pollen, extending their lifespan significantly.

snowflake-butterfly._en_desc: The snowflake butterfly is a delicate white butterfly found in tropical forests. Its mostly white wings with small dark tips give it a graceful appearance as it glides through forest understory.

resurrection-butterfly._en_desc: The resurrection butterfly, known as Kuroneko Yamane in Japan, is a medium-sized butterfly with distinctive markings. It has deep cultural significance in Japan as a symbol of love and resurrection.

cabbage-white-butterfly._en_desc: The small white butterfly is a widespread species often found in gardens and agricultural areas. Its caterpillars are major pests of cabbage and other brassica crops.

atlas-beetle._en_desc: The atlas beetle is a large rhinoceros beetle native to Southeast Asian rainforests. Males have three prominent horns used in combat for mates, and they are among the strongest insects relative to size.

goliath-beetle._en_desc: The goliath beetle is one of the largest and heaviest insects on Earth, found in African tropical forests. They feed on fruit and tree sap, and their larvae are among the heaviest grubs known.

rhinoceros-beetle._en_desc: The western hercules beetle is a large rhinoceros beetle found in the hardwood forests of North America. Males have a distinctive horn used for wrestling other males during mating season.

stag-beetle._en_desc: Stag beetles are named for the large, antler-like mandibles of the males. They spend most of their lives as larvae feeding on decaying wood underground before emerging as impressive adults.

dung-beetle._en_desc: Dung beetles roll animal droppings into balls for food or breeding. They are essential decomposers that help recycle nutrients back into the soil and reduce parasite populations in pastures.

ladybug._en_desc: Ladybugs are small, round beetles valued by gardeners for their appetite for aphids and other plant pests. Their bright red coloration with black spots warns predators of their bitter taste.

tiger-beetle._en_desc: Tiger beetles are fast-running predatory beetles with large eyes and powerful jaws. They are voracious hunters of smaller insects and are often found on open, sunlit ground.

longhorn-beetle._en_desc: The Asian longhorned beetle is an invasive species that attacks a wide variety of hardwood trees. It has distinctive black and white markings and very long antennae that exceed its body length.

click-beetle._en_desc: Click beetles have a unique clicking mechanism on their thorax that allows them to snap and launch into the air when overturned. Their larvae, called wireworms, are important soil dwellers.

bombardier-beetle._en_desc: The bombardier beetle defends itself by ejecting a hot, noxious chemical spray from its abdomen with an audible pop. The spray reaches temperatures near boiling and repels predators effectively.

june-bug._en_desc: June bugs are chunky, brown beetles that emerge in late spring. They are attracted to lights at night and their larvae, known as white grubs, feed on grass roots and can damage lawns.

whirligig-beetle._en_desc: Whirligig beetles are aquatic beetles that spin rapidly on the surface of calm water. They have split eyes adapted for both aerial and aquatic vision and are social insects that form groups.

diving-beetle._en_desc: Predaceous diving beetles are streamlined aquatic predators that hunt tadpoles, small fish, and other insects underwater. They trap air beneath their elytra for extended submerged hunting.

oil-beetle._en_desc: Oil beetles are flightless blister beetles that produce cantharidin, a toxic oily substance, from their joints. Their larvae parasitize solitary bees and develop inside their nests.

bess-beetle._en_desc: Bess beetles are large, shiny black beetles that live in decaying wood. They exhibit parental care, with adults feeding and caring for their larvae, which is unusual for beetles.

bark-beetle._en_desc: Mountain pine beetles are tiny bark beetles that bore into pine trees and introduce blue-stain fungi. Massive outbreaks have devastated millions of acres of forest in western North America.

sacred-scarab-beetle._en_desc: The sacred scarab beetle rolls dung into balls and was revered in ancient Egyptian culture as a symbol of rebirth and the sun's daily journey across the sky.

carrion-beetle._en_desc: The American carrion beetle is a large, flat beetle that feeds on dead animals and snails. It plays an important ecological role in recycling nutrients back into the ecosystem.

patrol-bess-beetle._en_desc: The patrol bess beetle is a large, glossy black beetle found in tropical rainforests. Like other passalid beetles, both parents work together to feed and care for their larvae.

eyed-click-beetle._en_desc: The eyed click beetle is a large click beetle with distinctive eyespots on its pronotum. When threatened, it clicks and flips into the air to right itself or escape danger.

rose-chafer._en_desc: The rose chafer is a metallic green beetle that feeds on flowers, especially roses and fruit blossoms. Despite being considered a pest, its larvae help decompose organic matter in soil.

japanese-beetle._en_desc: The Japanese beetle is a highly invasive pest that skeletonizes leaves and damages turf with its white grub larvae. It is native to Japan and has become a devastating pest in North America.

colorado-potato-beetle._en_desc: The Colorado potato beetle is a major agricultural pest that feeds on potatoes, tomatoes, and eggplants. It has developed resistance to over 50 different insecticides.

lily-beetle._en_desc: The scarlet lily beetle is a bright red pest of lily plants. Both adults and larvae feed on leaves, stems, and flowers, and the larvae cover themselves in their own excrement for protection.

elm-beetle._en_desc: The elm leaf beetle skeletonizes elm tree leaves and is a significant urban pest. Adults often overwinter inside buildings, emerging in spring to feed on newly emerged elm leaves.

fire-ant._en_desc: Red imported fire ants are invasive ants native to South America that deliver painful stings causing burning welts. They build large mound nests and can survive flooding by forming floating colonies.

leafcutter-ant._en_desc: Leafcutter ants cut and carry pieces of leaves back to their nests to feed a special fungus that they cultivate. They are sophisticated farmers with complex division of labor among castes.

bullet-ant._en_desc: The bullet ant gets its name from the intense pain of its sting, which has been compared to being shot. Indigenous tribes use bullet ant stings in coming-of-age rituals.

army-ant._en_desc: Army ants are nomadic predators that form massive raiding swarms. They do not build permanent nests but instead form living bivouacs made of their own bodies while the colony rests.

trap-jaw-ant._en_desc: Trap-jaw ants have spring-loaded mandibles that snap shut at incredible speeds to capture prey and can also use the force to launch themselves into the air to escape predators.

weaver-ant._en_desc: Weaver ants build elaborate nests by weaving living leaves together using silk produced by their larvae. They are aggressive defenders of their territory and tend honeydew-producing insects.

honeybee._en_desc: The western honeybee is the world's most important pollinator of agricultural crops. They live in highly organized colonies with complex social structures and produce honey and beeswax.

bumblebee._en_desc: Bumblebees are robust, fuzzy bees important for pollinating wildflowers and crops. They are capable of buzz pollination, vibrating their flight muscles to release pollen from flowers.

carpenter-bee._en_desc: Carpenter bees are large, solitary bees that bore into untreated wood to create nesting tunnels. Despite their intimidating size, they are gentle and rarely sting, preferring to hover near structures.

paper-wasp._en_desc: Paper wasps are slender wasps with long legs that build open-comb umbrella-shaped nests from wood pulp. They are beneficial predators of caterpillars but will sting if their nest is threatened.

yellow-jacket._en_desc: Yellow jackets are aggressive wasps known for their bright yellow and black markings. They build enclosed paper nests and are notorious for scavenging at picnics and outdoor events.

bald-faced-hornet._en_desc: Despite its name, the bald-faced hornet is actually a yellowjacket, not a true hornet. It builds large, enclosed paper nests high in trees and is known for its aggressive defense of its colony.

european-hornet._en_desc: The European hornet is the largest social wasp in Europe and an invasive species in North America. Queens can reach 1.4 inches in length, and colonies can contain up to 1,000 workers.

tarantula-hawk-wasp._en_desc: The tarantula hawk is a large, metallic blue-black wasp that hunts tarantulas to serve as live food for its larvae. Its sting is excruciatingly painful but rarely dangerous to humans.

cuckoo-wasp._en_desc: Cuckoo wasps are brilliant metallic blue or green parasitoids that lay their eggs in the nests of other bees and wasps. Their larvae consume the host's eggs or larvae and stored food.

ichneumon-wasp._en_desc: Giant ichneumon wasps are parasitoids that use their extremely long ovipositors to drill into wood and lay eggs inside wood-boring beetle larvae. Despite their fearsome appearance, they cannot sting humans.

asian-giant-hornet._en_desc: The Asian giant hornet, nicknamed the murder hornet, is the world's largest hornet. Its powerful sting delivers potent venom and it is a devastating predator of honeybee colonies.

sweat-bee._en_desc: Sweat bees are small, often metallic-colored bees attracted to human perspiration for its salt content. They are important pollinators and nest in the ground or in hollow stems.

mason-bee._en_desc: The blue orchard mason bee is a solitary bee that nests in hollow tubes and crevices. It is a far more efficient pollinator than honeybees, visiting far more flowers per hour.

mining-bee._en_desc: Mining bees are solitary ground-nesting bees that excavate tunnels in soil. They emerge in spring and are important early-season pollinators of fruit trees and wildflowers.

golden-digger-wasp._en_desc: The golden digger wasp is a large, metallic golden wasp that hunts grasshoppers and crickets. It buries paralyzed prey in underground nests for its developing larvae.

mud-dauber-wasp._en_desc: Mud dauber wasps are solitary wasps that construct tubular mud nests on sheltered surfaces. They hunt and paralyze spiders to stock each cell for their developing young.

horned-mason-bee._en_desc: The horned mason bee is a solitary bee that nests in hollow stems and bee hotels. Males have distinctive facial horns and both sexes are important early-season pollinators.

wool-carder-bee._en_desc: Wool carder bees are solitary bees that collect plant hairs to line their nest cells. Males aggressively defend patches of fuzzy plants where females forage for nesting material.

cicada-killer-wasp._en_desc: The cicada killer is a massive solitary wasp that hunts cicadas to provision its underground nest. Despite its intimidating size, it rarely stings humans unless provoked.

red-velvet-ant._en_desc: The red velvet ant is a wingless female wasp with a dense covering of bright red hairs. Despite its ant-like appearance, it is a parasitoid wasp whose sting is extremely painful.

cuckoo-bumblebee._en_desc: Cuckoo bumblebees are social parasites that take over the nests of other bumblebee species. The female cuckoo bumblebee displaces the host queen and lays her own eggs for the workers to tend.

mosquito._en_desc: The Asian tiger mosquito is an invasive species that can transmit dengue, chikungunya, and Zika viruses. It is identified by its distinctive black and white striped body and legs.

house-fly._en_desc: The common house fly is one of the most widespread insects, closely associated with humans. It has sponging mouthparts for liquid feeding and can transmit numerous diseases.

fruit-fly._en_desc: The common fruit fly is tiny but remarkably important in scientific research. They reproduce rapidly and share many genes with humans, making them invaluable for studying genetics and disease.

crane-fly._en_desc: Crane flies are delicate, long-legged insects that resemble oversized mosquitoes. Adults are harmless and many do not feed at all, while their larvae, known as leatherjackets, live in soil.

horsefly._en_desc: Horse flies are large, powerful fliers with razor-sharp mouthparts that slash skin to feed on blood. Only females bite, and their painful bites can transmit diseases to livestock and humans.

bot-fly._en_desc: The human bot fly is a parasitic insect whose larvae develop beneath the skin of mammals, including humans. Adults do not bite; instead, they hijack mosquitoes to deliver their eggs to hosts.

hover-fly._en_desc: Hover flies are beneficial pollinators that mimic the appearance of stinging insects for protection. Their larvae are important predators of aphids, making them valuable in pest control.

black-fly._en_desc: Black flies are tiny but relentless biting insects that breed in flowing water. In some regions they transmit river blindness and are considered one of the most important disease vectors.

damselfly._en_desc: Damselflies are slender, delicate relatives of dragonflies that hold their wings together above their body when resting. They are important aquatic ecosystem indicators and voracious mosquito predators.

blue-dasher-dragonfly._en_desc: The blue dasher is a small, common dragonfly with a blue-green body and distinctive wing pattern. It is an agile aerial predator that catches mosquitoes and other small insects on the wing.

emperor-dragonfly._en_desc: The emperor dragonfly is one of the largest and most powerful dragonflies in Europe. It patrols territories over water and feeds voraciously on mosquitoes, flies, and other flying insects.

four-spotted-chaser._en_desc: The four-spotted chaser is a robust dragonfly with distinctive dark spots on its wings. It is an aggressive territorial species that perches on vegetation to ambush passing prey.

robber-fly._en_desc: Robber flies are aerial predators that intercept prey in flight. They inject victims with saliva that paralyzes and digests their insides, then suck out the liquefied contents.

marmalade-hoverfly._en_desc: The marmalade hoverfly is a bee-mimic hoverfly that is an important pollinator. Its larvae are voracious aphid predators, making it doubly valuable in gardens and agriculture.

common-mosquito._en_desc: Mosquitoes are small, buzzing flies that transmit deadly diseases including malaria, dengue, and Zika. Only females bite to obtain blood for egg production, while males feed on nectar.

biting-midge._en_desc: Biting midges are tiny flies that deliver disproportionately painful bites. They are among the smallest biting flies and can be major pests in coastal and tropical regions.

deer-fly._en_desc: Deer flies are fast-flying, aggressive biters with patterned wings. They transmit tularemia and can cause severe allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

cattle-bot-fly._en_desc: The cattle bot fly is a parasitic fly whose larvae develop in the throats of cattle. Adults are bee-like in appearance and do not feed, living only long enough to reproduce.

orchid-mantis._en_desc: The orchid mantis is a stunning pink and white mantis that mimics orchid flowers to ambush pollinators. It is considered one of the most beautiful insects in the world.

ghost-mantis._en_desc: The ghost mantis is a master of camouflage with a body shaped and colored to resemble a dried leaf. It sways gently to mimic a leaf in the wind, hiding from both predators and prey.

leaf-mantis._en_desc: The dead leaf mantis is a large, spectacular mantis with a flattened body resembling a dead leaf. It is an ambush predator that waits motionless for prey to come within striking distance.

walking-stick._en_desc: Walking sticks are elongated, camouflaged insects that resemble twigs or branches. They are nocturnal herbivores that rely on their extraordinary disguise to avoid detection by predators.

giant-walking-stick._en_desc: The giant walking stick, also known as Chan's megastick, is the longest insect species, with females reaching over 14 inches including legs. It is native to Borneo's tropical rainforests.

american-cockroach._en_desc: The American cockroach is the largest common cockroach found in human habitations. Despite its name, it originated in Africa and is now found worldwide in warm, moist environments.

german-cockroach._en_desc: The German cockroach is the most troublesome indoor cockroach species worldwide. It reproduces rapidly, is resistant to many insecticides, and contaminates food and surfaces with pathogens.

madagascar-hissing-cockroach._en_desc: The Madagascar hissing cockroach is one of the largest cockroach species, reaching 3 inches long. It is famous for the loud hissing sound it produces when disturbed, used for defense and communication.

oriental-cockroach._en_desc: The oriental cockroach is a large, dark species that prefers cool, damp environments. It is a scavenger that feeds on decaying organic matter and is associated with poor sanitation.

eastern-subterranean-termite._en_desc: Eastern subterranean termites are the most destructive termite species in North America. They live in underground colonies and build mud tubes to reach wood structures above ground.

formosan-termite._en_desc: The Formosan termite is one of the most destructive termite species, capable of consuming enormous amounts of wood. Unlike most termites, it can build above-ground nests, making it especially destructive.

dampwood-termite._en_desc: Dampwood termites infest moist, decaying wood and are indicators of excessive moisture problems. They are larger than subterranean termites and do not build mud tubes.

drywood-termite._en_desc: Drywood termites live entirely within the wood they consume and do not require soil contact. They are difficult to detect and treat because colonies can be scattered throughout a structure.

cicada._en_desc: Periodical cicadas are famous for their synchronized mass emergences every 13 or 17 years. They are the longest-lived insects and their emergences create deafening choruses heard for miles.

dog-day-cicada._en_desc: Dog-day cicadas are annual cicadas that emerge each summer, unlike their periodical cousins. Their loud buzzing songs fill late summer afternoons in eastern North America.

masked-devil-cicada._en_desc: The masked devil cicada is an Australian species known for its distinctive facial markings. Like other cicadas, it spends years underground before emerging for a brief, noisy adult life.

leafhopper._en_desc: The brown planthopper is a major pest of rice crops in Asia. It feeds on plant sap and transmits the devastating rice ragged stunt virus and rice grassy stunt virus.

spittlebug._en_desc: Spittlebugs get their name from the frothy foam masses their nymphs produce on plant stems. These nymphs, called froghoppers, are sap-sucking insects that can transmit plant diseases.

aphid._en_desc: The green peach aphid is one of the most destructive agricultural pests worldwide. It reproduces rapidly through asexual reproduction and transmits over 100 plant viruses.

bed-bug._en_desc: Bed bugs are parasitic insects that feed on human blood at night. They hide in mattress seams, furniture, and wall cracks, and their populations have surged worldwide due to pesticide resistance.

kissing-bug._en_desc: Triatomine bugs, also known as kissing bugs, are vectors of Chagas disease. They feed on blood at night and transmit the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi through their feces.

stink-bug._en_desc: The brown marmorated stink bug is an invasive species from Asia that has become a major agricultural pest in North America. It damages fruit crops and invades homes in winter seeking shelter.

box-elder-bug._en_desc: Box elder bugs are black insects with red markings that feed on box elder tree seeds. They become nuisances in fall when they cluster on buildings seeking warmth for winter.

water-strider._en_desc: Water striders are insects that glide across the surface of calm water using surface tension. Their hydrophobic leg hairs create air cushions that keep them afloat while they hunt prey.

giant-water-bug._en_desc: Giant water bugs are large, flat-bodied aquatic predators that prey on fish, frogs, and snakes. Males carry eggs on their backs and are sometimes called electric-light bugs for their attraction to lights.

american-grasshopper._en_desc: The American bird grasshopper is a large, strong-flying grasshopper that feeds on a wide variety of plants. It gets its name from its bird-like flight and large size.

desert-locust._en_desc: The desert locust is the most destructive of all locust species. Under certain conditions it transforms from a solitary grasshopper into a gregarious swarming phase capable of devastating crops.

mormon-cricket._en_desc: The Mormon cricket is not a cricket but a large shield-backed katydid that forms migrating bands of billions. They were named after Mormon settlers whose crops they devastated in the 1840s.

field-cricket._en_desc: Field crickets are known for their distinctive chirping songs produced by males to attract mates. They are omnivorous scavengers that feed on plants, fungi, and other insects.

katydid._en_desc: True katydids are named after their call, said to sound like Katy-did, Katy-didn't. They are leaf-mimicking insects that produce loud, clicking songs at ultrasonic frequencies.

mole-cricket._en_desc: Mole crickets are burrowing insects with powerful, shovel-like forelegs adapted for digging through soil. They damage lawns and crops by feeding on roots and disrupting soil structure.

snowy-tree-cricket._en_desc: The snowy tree cricket produces a pure, musical trill and is famous for its temperature-dependent chirping rate. Dolbear's Law uses its chirps to estimate ambient temperature.

human-head-louse._en_desc: Human head lice are parasitic insects that live on the scalp and feed on blood. They are wingless and highly adapted to life on humans, spreading through direct head-to-head contact.

body-louse._en_desc: Human body lice live in clothing and emerge to feed on blood. Unlike head lice, they can transmit serious diseases including typhus, trench fever, and relapsing fever.

human-flea._en_desc: The human flea, Pulex irritans, is the original flea species associated with humans. It is a blood-feeding parasite that can transmit diseases and has been a companion of humans for millennia.

cat-flea._en_desc: The cat flea is the most common flea species affecting domestic cats and dogs. Despite its name, it infests many mammal species and can cause allergic dermatitis and transmit tapeworms.

oriental-rat-flea._en_desc: The oriental rat flea is historically the most important disease vector among fleas, having transmitted bubonic plague during the Black Death. It feeds primarily on rats and other rodents.

brown-recluse-spider._en_desc: The brown recluse spider has a violin-shaped marking on its cephalothorax and venom that can cause tissue death. It is reclusive and bites only when pressed against skin.

wolf-spider._en_desc: Wolf spiders are agile, ground-hunting spiders that do not build webs. They have excellent vision and chase down their prey, and females are notable for carrying their young on their backs.

jumping-spider._en_desc: Bold jumping spiders are charismatic, fuzzy spiders with large forward-facing eyes. They are active hunters that stalk prey and leap to capture it, displaying complex courtship dances.

orb-weaver-spider._en_desc: Garden orb weavers are among the most common web-building spiders. They create distinctive circular webs and are beneficial predators of flying insects in gardens and natural areas.

peacock-spider._en_desc: Peacock spiders are tiny jumping spiders famous for the males' spectacular iridescent abdominal flaps used in elaborate courtship dances. Females will eat males who fail to impress.

brazilian-wandering-spider._en_desc: The Brazilian wandering spider is considered the world's most venomous spider. Unlike web-building spiders, it actively wanders the forest floor at night and can deliver a medically significant bite.

emperor-scorpion._en_desc: The emperor scorpion is one of the largest scorpion species and one of the most popular in the pet trade. Despite its intimidating size, its venom is relatively mild and it is generally docile.

bark-scorpion._en_desc: The Arizona bark scorpion is the most dangerous scorpion in North America. It is unique among scorpions in its ability to climb walls and ceilings, often entering homes through plumbing.

deathstalker-scorpion._en_desc: The deathstalker is one of the most venomous scorpions in the world. Its potent neurotoxic venom can be fatal to humans, but its venom compounds show promise in medical research.

spotted-lanternfly._en_desc: The spotted lanternfly is an invasive planthopper from Asia that feeds on over 70 plant species, threatening agriculture. Adults have distinctive spotted wings and bright red hind wings.

wheel-bug._en_desc: The wheel bug is a large, beneficial predatory insect with a distinctive semicircular crest on its thorax. It uses its proboscis to inject digestive enzymes into prey and is a natural pest controller.

sawfly._en_desc: Sawflies are wasp-like insects whose larvae feed on plant foliage, resembling caterpillars. The rose slug sawfly can skeletonize rose leaves, causing significant damage to gardens.

antlion._en_desc: Antlions are insects whose larvae are famous for digging conical pitfall traps in sand. They wait at the bottom of the pit for prey to fall in, then inject digestive enzymes.

lacewing._en_desc: Green lacewings are delicate, golden-green insects with lace-like wings. Their larvae are voracious predators of aphids and other soft-bodied pests, making them valuable biological control agents.

dobsonfly._en_desc: The eastern dobsonfly is a large, impressive insect with enormous wings and males have extremely long mandibles. The aquatic larvae are important food for trout and indicators of stream health.

mayfly._en_desc: Mayflies are aquatic insects with extremely short adult lifespans dedicated solely to reproduction. Their larvae are important indicators of water quality and food for fish.

earwig._en_desc: The common European earwig is a nocturnal insect with distinctive pincer-like cerci on its abdomen. Despite myths, earwigs do not burrow into human ears, and mothers provide notable parental care.

silverfish._en_desc: Silverfish are small, wingless, silver-colored insects that damage paper, textiles, and food. They are nocturnal and thrive in warm, humid environments like bathrooms and basements.

firebrat._en_desc: Firebrats are close relatives of silverfish that prefer much warmer environments. They are found near heat sources like furnaces and water heaters and feed on starchy materials.

jumping-bristletail._en_desc: Jumping bristletails are small, wingless insects that can jump by curling their abdomen. They are found in moist environments and feed on algae, lichens, and decaying plant matter.

snakefly._en_desc: Snakeflies are predatory insects with an elongated prothorax that gives them a snake-like appearance. Both adults and larvae are beneficial predators of pest insects on trees.

cuckoo-bumblebee-parasite._en_desc: This cuckoo bumblebee species is a social parasite that takes over nests of other bumblebee species. The female enters a host nest, kills or displaces the queen, and uses the existing workers.

musk-bee._en_desc: The musk bee is a solitary ground-nesting bee known for its distinctive musky scent. It emerges in late summer and is an important pollinator of goldenrod and other fall wildflowers.

alkali-bee._en_desc: The alkali bee is a solitary ground-nesting bee that prefers alkaline soils near salt flats. It is an excellent pollinator of alfalfa and has been managed commercially for this purpose.

carpenter-ant._en_desc: Black carpenter ants are large ants that excavate nests in moist, decaying wood. Unlike termites, they do not consume wood but can cause structural damage by hollowing out timbers.

pharaoh-ant._en_desc: Pharaoh ants are tiny, pale-colored invasive ants that are particularly problematic in hospitals and food facilities. They form huge colonies with multiple queens and bud frequently.

odorous-house-ant._en_desc: Odorous house ants are common household ants that emit a distinctive coconut-like odor when crushed. They form large colonies and frequently nest inside walls and under floors.

blue-ringed-octopus._en_desc: The blue-ringed octopus is a small but deadly cephalopod native to coral reefs. Despite its diminutive size, its bright blue rings serve as a warning of its highly potent venom.

mimic-octopus._en_desc: The mimic octopus is a master of disguise, capable of altering its shape, color, and behavior to resemble other marine animals. It was only discovered in 1998 off the coast of Indonesia.

colossal-squid._en_desc: The colossal squid is one of the largest invertebrates on Earth, inhabiting the frigid deep waters of the Antarctic. Its massive eyes are adapted to detect light in the perpetual darkness of the deep sea.

humboldt-squid._en_desc: The Humboldt squid is a large, aggressive cephalopod named after the Humboldt Current. It hunts in packs and is known for its rapid growth rate and voracious appetite.

giant-squid._en_desc: The giant squid is one of the most mysterious creatures of the deep ocean. With eyes the size of dinner plates and tentacles reaching over 40 feet, it is a legendary predator of the abyss.

firefly-squid._en_desc: The firefly squid is a small cephalopod famous for its bioluminescence. Each spring millions gather in Toyama Bay, Japan, creating a spectacular natural light show.

caribbean-reef-octopus._en_desc: The Caribbean reef octopus is a nocturnal predator that hunts crustaceans and small fish among coral formations. Its chromatophores allow rapid color changes for communication and camouflage.

flamboyant-cuttlefish._en_desc: The flamboyant cuttlefish is a small, vibrantly colored cephalopod that walks along the seafloor on its tentacles. It displays pulsating patterns of yellow, maroon, and white as a warning to predators.

common-cuttlefish._en_desc: The common cuttlefish is a highly intelligent cephalopod with W-shaped pupils and an internal cuttlebone used for buoyancy. It is renowned for its extraordinary ability to change color and texture.

chambered-nautilus._en_desc: The chambered nautilus is a cephalopod often called a living fossil, having existed since before the dinosaurs. Its beautiful spiral shell is divided into chambers used for buoyancy control.

argonaut._en_desc: The argonaut, or paper nautilus, is a pelagic octopus where only females produce a delicate calcareous shell. Males are much smaller and lack shells entirely.

vampire-squid._en_desc: The vampire squid inhabits the deep ocean's oxygen minimum zones. Despite its name, it feeds on marine snow rather than prey, and can turn itself inside out as a defense mechanism.

strawberry-squid._en_desc: The strawberry squid is a deep-sea cephalopod covered in light-producing photophores. Its red coloring is invisible in the deep ocean, providing effective camouflage against predators.

cockatoo-squid._en_desc: The cockatoo squid is a small, translucent deep-sea cephalopod that inflates its body like a balloon when threatened. Its distinctive appearance resembles a cockatoo with its arms raised.

pajama-squid._en_desc: The pajama squid is a small, nocturnal cephalopod with distinctive black and white stripes. It buries itself in sand during the day and emerges at night to hunt small crustaceans.

bobtail-squid._en_desc: Bobtail squids are small, round cephalopods that partner with bioluminescent bacteria. The bacteria produce light that matches the moonlight from above, eliminating the squid's shadow.

pygmy-squid._en_desc: The pygmy squid is one of the smallest cephalopods, reaching barely an inch long. It uses a special adhesive gland to attach itself to seagrass blades, waiting to ambush passing prey.

american-lobster._en_desc: The American lobster is a large marine crustacean prized as a delicacy. It uses its powerful claws for defense and crushing prey, and can regenerate lost limbs during molting.

european-lobster._en_desc: The European lobster is a large, deep-blue crustacean found along rocky coastlines. It is a solitary nocturnal hunter that preys on fish, crabs, and mollusks.

spiny-lobster._en_desc: Spiny lobsters are colorful crustaceans found in tropical marine environments. Unlike true lobsters, they lack large front claws and instead rely on their spiny antennae and a unique alarm call.

slipper-lobster._en_desc: Slipper lobsters are robust crustaceans recognized by their flattened, slipper-shaped antennae. They are bottom-dwellers that hunt mollusks and other invertebrates at night.

mantis-shrimp._en_desc: The mantis shrimp is a strikingly colored crustacean with the fastest punch in the animal kingdom. It possesses the most complex eyes known, with 16 types of color receptors compared to humans' three.

peacock-mantis-shrimp._en_desc: The peacock mantis shrimp is one of the most colorful and formidable predators in the reef. Its club-like appendages strike with incredible speed and force, capable of shattering glass aquariums.

spearer-mantis-shrimp._en_desc: Spearer mantis shrimp are ambush predators that wait at the entrance of their mud burrows. They strike passing prey with barbed, spear-like appendages that can impale fish in milliseconds.

blue-crab._en_desc: The blue crab is a commercially important species found along the Atlantic coast of North America. It is an aggressive swimmer and opportunistic feeder that plays a key role in estuarine ecosystems.

king-crab._en_desc: The red king crab is one of the largest crabs in the world, prized commercially in Alaska and Russia. Its massive, spiny legs can span over five feet and it can walk up to 100 miles during its annual migration.

japanese-spider-crab._en_desc: The Japanese spider crab holds the record for the largest leg span of any living arthropod. Despite its enormous size, it is a gentle giant that scavenges on the ocean floor.

hermit-crab._en_desc: Hermit crabs are decapod crustaceans that use abandoned snail shells to protect their soft abdomens. They are social animals often found in groups, and play dead when threatened.

coconut-crab._en_desc: The coconut crab is the largest terrestrial arthropod, capable of cracking coconuts with its powerful claws. Despite its name, it lives primarily on land but must return to the sea to reproduce.

snow-crab._en_desc: The snow crab is a cold-water species that lives on sandy and muddy bottoms. It is an important commercial species in both the Atlantic and Pacific, known for its sweet, tender meat.

fiddler-crab._en_desc: Fiddler crabs are small semiterrestrial crabs recognized by the male's single oversized claw used in elaborate mating dances. They are important ecosystem engineers in mangrove and marsh habitats.

mud-crab._en_desc: The mud crab is a robust species found in mangrove ecosystems across the Indo-Pacific. It is one of the most commercially important crabs in aquaculture, prized for its sweet, firm meat.

atlantic-ghost-crab._en_desc: Ghost crabs are pale, fast-moving crustaceans that burrow in sandy beaches. They are mostly nocturnal and use their large stalked eyes and acute hearing to detect predators and prey.

tropical-hermit-crab._en_desc: Tropical hermit crabs are colorful land-dwelling crustaceans that inhabit beaches and coastal forests. They are highly social and often form shell exchange chains to ensure all members have appropriate shelter.

coconut-hermit-crab._en_desc: The coconut hermit crab is a large land-dwelling species that inhabits tropical island beaches. It is known for its habit of using coconut shells as mobile homes and feeding on fallen coconuts.

zebra-fiddler-crab._en_desc: The zebra fiddler crab is named for the distinctive stripes on its carapace. Males perform elaborate claw-waving displays to attract females and defend territory on tropical mudflats.

great-spider-crab._en_desc: The great spider crab is a camouflaged crustacean that attaches organisms to its shell for disguise. It migrates in large numbers to shallow waters for mating each autumn.

swimming-crab._en_desc: Swimming crabs are agile crustaceans with modified rear legs that function as paddles. They are aggressive predators that can pursue prey through the water column with remarkable speed.

common-shore-shrimp._en_desc: Common shore shrimp are small crustaceans inhabiting the turbulent intertidal zone. They use specialized appendages to cling to rocks and forage among algae and barnacles for food.

antarctic-krill._en_desc: Antarctic krill are small crustaceans that form the foundation of the Antarctic marine food web. Swarms can contain billions of individuals and are a critical food source for whales, seals, and penguins.

pacific-krill._en_desc: Pacific krill are tiny shrimp-like crustaceans that swarm in massive numbers in the North Pacific. They are essential to the marine food web, feeding on phytoplankton and being consumed by larger marine life.

atlantic-krill._en_desc: Atlantic krill are small pelagic crustaceans found throughout the North Atlantic. They are a keystone species, supporting populations of cod, herring, whales, and numerous seabirds.

giant-amphipod._en_desc: Giant amphipods are deep-sea crustaceans found in ocean trenches up to 10,000 meters deep. Their enormous size compared to shallow-water relatives is an example of deep-sea gigantism.

giant-isopod._en_desc: Giant isopods are deep-sea crustaceans that can grow up to 14 inches long. They are scavengers that feed on whale falls and other organic material that sinks to the ocean floor.

lions-mane-jellyfish._en_desc: The lion's mane jellyfish is the largest known jellyfish species. Its mass of long, trailing tentacles resembles a lion's mane and can extend far beyond its bell diameter.

portuguese-man-of-war._en_desc: The Portuguese man-of-war is a siphonophore, not a true jellyfish. Its iconic blue float sails on the surface while trailing long, venomous tentacles that can deliver an extremely painful sting.

pacific-sea-nettle._en_desc: The Pacific sea nettle is a large, visually striking jellyfish with a rusty-orange bell and long, coiling tentacles. It feeds on zooplankton, fish eggs, and other jellyfish.

upside-down-jellyfish._en_desc: The upside-down jellyfish, or Cassiopea, lies bell-down on the substrate to maximize photosynthesis by its symbiotic algae. It pulses gently to circulate water and capture food particles.

immortal-jellyfish._en_desc: The immortal jellyfish, Turritopsis dohrnii, is biologically immortal. When stressed or aging, it reverts to its polyp form and begins its life cycle anew, making it the only known creature capable of true rejuvenation.

sea-wasp._en_desc: The sea wasp, or Chironex fleckeri, is the largest and most dangerous box jellyfish. Its nearly invisible body and incredibly potent venom make it one of the deadliest creatures in the ocean.

compass-jellyfish._en_desc: The compass jellyfish is easily identified by the brown radiating lines on its translucent bell that resemble compass markings. It feeds on small fish and other jellyfish.

fried-egg-jellyfish._en_desc: The fried egg jellyfish, or Cotylorhiza tuberculata, is a visually striking species with a bell that looks remarkably like a fried egg. Despite its large size, its sting is relatively mild.

blood-belly-comb-jelly._en_desc: The blood belly comb jelly is a deep-water ctenophore found in the Mediterranean. When threatened, it produces vivid red bioluminescence, creating a spectacular display in the dark waters.

atolla-jellyfish._en_desc: The Atolla jellyfish inhabits the deep ocean and is famous for its burglar alarm display. When attacked, it produces a rotating wheel of blue bioluminescence to attract larger predators that may attack its attacker.

spotted-jelly._en_desc: The spotted jelly is a rhizostome jellyfish with a translucent bell covered in brown spots. It feeds on plankton and small organisms using oral arms lined with tiny mouth openings.

mauve-stinger._en_desc: The mauve stinger is a deep-water jellyfish with a distinctive reddish-purple bell covered in nematocyst clusters. It forms massive blooms in open ocean waters.

staghorn-coral._en_desc: Staghorn coral is a critically endangered branching coral species. Once dominant in Caribbean reefs, its populations have declined by over 80% due to disease, bleaching, and predation.

brain-coral._en_desc: Brain coral is named for its spherical shape and the winding grooves on its surface that resemble a human brain. It is a slow-growing but extremely long-lived reef-building species.

elkhorn-coral._en_desc: Elkhorn coral is a critically endangered species that once formed vast reefs throughout the Caribbean. Its large, branching colonies provide essential habitat for hundreds of reef species.

pillar-coral._en_desc: Pillar coral is one of the rarest reef-building corals, distinguished by its tall, cylindrical columns that rise from the reef. It is listed as critically endangered with populations plummeting.

fire-coral._en_desc: Fire coral is a colony-forming hydrozoan that looks like true coral but delivers a painful sting on contact. Its smooth, branching colonies are typically brown, yellow, or reddish in color.

blue-coral._en_desc: Blue coral is a unique reef-building species with a distinctive blue skeleton. It is one of the few corals that can survive in turbid, low-light environments where other corals cannot.

mushroom-coral._en_desc: Mushroom corals are solitary, free-living scleractinian corals shaped like mushrooms. Unlike colonial species, each is a single polyp that can detach and roll across the substrate.

black-coral._en_desc: Black corals are deep-water colonial organisms with a black or dark brown skeleton. They are among the longest-lived organisms on Earth, with some colonies surviving for millennia.

sea-pen._en_desc: Sea pens are colonial cnidarians that resemble old-fashioned quill pens. They anchor in soft sediment and can produce bioluminescent waves of light that travel along their colonies.

sea-whip._en_desc: Sea whips are octocoral colonies that grow in long, whip-like branches. They are filter feeders that extend polyps into the current to capture plankton and organic particles.

sunflower-sea-star._en_desc: The sunflower sea star is one of the largest and fastest sea stars, but populations have crashed by over 90% due to sea star wasting disease. It is now listed as critically endangered.

crown-of-thorns-starfish._en_desc: The crown-of-thorns starfish is a large, multi-armed sea star covered in venomous spines. It is a significant coral predator whose population outbreaks can devastate reef ecosystems.

blue-sea-star._en_desc: The blue sea star is a strikingly colored echinoderm that lives on sandy substrates. It feeds on small invertebrates buried in the sand and can regenerate lost arms.

leather-star._en_desc: The leather star is a smooth-skinned sea star found on rocky reefs. It has a distinctive reddish-brown color and a unique garlic-like odor when handled.

common-brittle-star._en_desc: Brittle stars are echinoderms with a distinct central disc and five long, slender arms. They are more agile than sea stars, moving by writhing their arms across the seabed.

giant-basket-star._en_desc: The giant basket star is a spectacular echinoderm with a complex network of branching arms. At night, it unfurls its arms into the current to capture plankton and small crustaceans.

feather-star._en_desc: Feather stars are mobile crinoids that cling to coral or swim through the water column. Their feathery arms filter plankton from passing currents, and they can detach to relocate when conditions change.

crinoid-feather-star._en_desc: Crinoid feather stars are ancient echinoderms related to sea lilies. They perch on coral heads and wave their feathery arms to capture passing plankton from ocean currents.

disk-brittle-star._en_desc: The disk-brittle star is a small, agile echinoderm found in rock crevices and under stones. It is an opportunistic feeder that can regenerate lost body parts rapidly.

purple-sea-urchin._en_desc: The purple sea urchin is a spiny echinoderm that inhabits rocky shores. It uses its five-toothed jaw, Aristotle's lantern, to scrape algae and even excavate burrows in solid rock.

long-spined-sea-urchin._en_desc: Long-spined sea urchins are tropical echinoderms with extremely long, sharp spines that provide excellent defense. They play a critical role in controlling algal growth on coral reefs.

pencil-urchin._en_desc: Pencil urchins are named for their thick, cylindrical spines that look like colored pencils. They inhabit tropical reefs where they graze on algae using their complex jaw apparatus.

green-sea-urchin._en_desc: The green sea urchin is a cold-water species found on rocky substrates. It is an important herbivore in kelp forest ecosystems, controlling algal growth and providing food for sea otters.

flower-urchin._en_desc: The flower urchin is one of the most dangerous sea urchins, covered in venomous flower-shaped pedicellariae. Despite its beautiful appearance, contact causes intense pain and potential tissue damage.

sand-dollar._en_desc: Sand dollars are flat, burrowing sea urchins found on sandy ocean floors. Their flattened bodies and fine spines allow them to bury themselves just beneath the sediment surface.

carpenter-sea-urchin._en_desc: The carpenter sea urchin is named for its ability to excavate burrows in solid coral rock. Its powerful Aristotle's lantern allows it to bore into reef substrates for shelter.

fire-urchin._en_desc: The fire urchin is a striking red echinoderm with venomous spines that deliver an intensely painful sting. Despite its danger, it provides a symbiotic home for certain shrimp and crabs.

slate-pencil-urchin._en_desc: Slate pencil urchins are named for their thick, blunt spines that resemble slate pencils. These colorful echinoderms inhabit tropical reefs where they graze on algae.

tiger-tail-sea-cucumber._en_desc: The tiger tail sea cucumber is a large, conspicuous species with distinctive dark stripes. It is an important bioturbator, processing sediment and recycling nutrients in tropical marine ecosystems.

lolly-sea-cucumber._en_desc: The lolly sea cucumber is a small, cylindrical species that processes sand and sediment on tropical reefs. It plays a vital role in reef health by recycling organic matter.

pacific-sea-cucumber._en_desc: The Pacific sea cucumber is an ecologically important detritivore that processes vast quantities of sediment. It is commercially harvested and considered a culinary delicacy in many Asian cultures.

black-sea-cucumber._en_desc: The black sea cucumber is a large, commercially valuable species found on tropical reefs. It ejects its internal organs as a defense mechanism and later regenerates them completely.

teatfish-sea-cucumber._en_desc: The teatfish is a large, highly valued sea cucumber that has been overexploited for the Asian beche-de-mer trade. Its distinctive nipple-like projections give it its common name.

red-sea-cucumber._en_desc: The red sea cucumber is a common species in Pacific kelp forests. It grazes on detritus and algae on rocky substrates, playing an important role in nutrient cycling.

christmas-tree-worm._en_desc: Christmas tree worms are tubeworms that burrow into living coral colonies. Their colorful, spiral-shaped radioles filter plankton from the water and can retract instantly when disturbed.

giant-tubeworm._en_desc: Giant tube worms are extraordinary deep-sea organisms that thrive at hydrothermal vents. They rely on chemosynthetic bacteria housed in a special organ called the trophosome for all nutrition.

feather-duster-worm._en_desc: Feather duster worms are sedentary polychaetes that construct tubes on reef surfaces. Their spectacular crown of feathery tentacles filters plankton and can retract rapidly when threatened.

bearded-fireworm._en_desc: The bearded fireworm is a predatory polychaete with venomous bristles called chaetae. Contact with these white, hair-like structures causes severe pain, inflammation, and numbness.

blue-glaucus._en_desc: The blue glaucus, or blue dragon, is a tiny, vibrant blue sea slug that floats upside-down on the ocean surface. It stores stinging cells from its prey for its own defense.

spanish-dancer._en_desc: The Spanish dancer is one of the largest and most colorful nudibranchs. When swimming, it unfurls its brilliant red and white mantle in a mesmerizing undulating display.

leaf-sheep._en_desc: The leaf sheep, or Costasiella kuroshimae, is a tiny sea slug that can photosynthesize like a plant. It steals chloroplasts from the algae it eats and stores them in its body to produce energy.

sea-butterfly._en_desc: Sea butterflies are tiny marine snails that swim through the open ocean by flapping their wing-like shell extensions. They are an important food source for fish, whales, and seabirds.

sea-angel._en_desc: Sea angels are gelatinous, transparent marine gastropods that lack shells. They swim through cold ocean waters by flapping wing-like appendages and prey on sea butterflies.

sea-hare._en_desc: The California sea hare is a large marine gastropod named for its ear-like rhinophores. It feeds on kelp and seaweed and can release a cloud of purple ink as a defense mechanism.

giant-clam._en_desc: The giant clam is the largest living bivalve mollusk, reaching over four feet in length. Its colorful mantle harbors symbiotic algae that provide much of its nutrition through photosynthesis.

geoduck._en_desc: The geoduck is the largest burrowing clam in the world, with a siphon that can extend three feet. Native to the Pacific Northwest, it is a prized delicacy in Asian cuisine.

atlantic-surf-clam._en_desc: The Atlantic surf clam is a large bivalve found on sandy substrates. It uses its powerful foot to burrow and can explosively eject itself from the sand when threatened by predators.

bay-scallop._en_desc: Bay scallops are small, fan-shaped bivalves that live in shallow coastal waters. Unlike most clams, they can swim by rapidly clapping their valves, ejecting water for propulsion.

blue-mussel._en_desc: Blue mussels are filter-feeding bivalves that attach to rocks with strong byssal threads. They form dense beds that provide habitat for numerous other species and are commercially cultivated.

thorny-oyster._en_desc: The thorny oyster is a large, spiny bivalve that cements itself to reef substrates. Its long, sharp spines protect it from predators and can cause painful wounds if touched.

lion-paw-scallop._en_desc: The lion paw scallop is a large, colorful bivalve with a distinctive ridged shell. It can swim by clapping its valves and is found in kelp forests along the Pacific coast.

nautilus-pompilius._en_desc: Nautilus pompilius is a cephalopod with a beautiful, spiraled shell that has inspired artists and mathematicians for centuries. It is a living fossil, virtually unchanged for 500 million years.

paper-nautilus._en_desc: The paper nautilus is an argonaut octopus in which only females produce a fragile, calcareous shell. Males are much smaller and shell-less, using a specialized arm to transfer sperm.

atlantic-horseshoe-crab._en_desc: The Atlantic horseshoe crab is a marine arthropod often called a living fossil. Despite its name, it is more closely related to spiders and scorpions than to true crabs.

japanese-horseshoe-crab._en_desc: The Japanese horseshoe crab is an endangered species whose unique blue blood is vital to modern medicine. The substance in its blood detects bacterial endotoxins in pharmaceuticals and medical devices.

indo-pacific-horseshoe-crab._en_desc: The Indo-Pacific horseshoe crab is an endangered marine arthropod found in Southeast Asian coastal waters. Like its Atlantic relative, it has blue blood containing valuable immune cells.

sea-squirt-tunicate._en_desc: Sea squirts are tunicates, marine invertebrates that are surprisingly closely related to vertebrates. As larvae they have a notochord, which they lose as adults when they attach to surfaces and become filter feeders.

marine-flatworm._en_desc: Marine flatworms are colorful, soft-bodied invertebrates that glide across reef surfaces. Despite their simple appearance, they are active predators that can deliver venomous bites.

sea-pen-glow._en_desc: The deep-sea pennatula is a species of sea pen that inhabits deep muddy bottoms. When disturbed, it produces stunning bioluminescent waves that ripple along its colony.

dodo._en_desc: The dodo was a large, flightless bird native to the island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean. It was related to pigeons and doves but evolved to be completely flightless with no natural predators.

woolly-mammoth._en_desc: The woolly mammoth was a species of elephant covered in thick fur that lived during the Pleistocene epoch. They roamed the cold tundra regions of North America, Europe, and Asia.

passenger-pigeon._en_desc: The passenger pigeon was once the most abundant bird in North America, with flocks containing billions of individuals. Systematic hunting and habitat destruction led to its extinction in 1914.

tasmanian-tiger._en_desc: The Tasmanian tiger, or thylacine, was a carnivorous marsupial native to Tasmania, Australia, and New Guinea. The last known individual died in captivity in 1936.

quagga._en_desc: The quagga was a subspecies of plains zebra that lived in South Africa. It was distinguished by its limited striping pattern, with stripes only on the head and front body.
